huli_honabe.name: Brings forth the first generation of deities and of the world's creatures
huli_honabe.notes: Primordial procreatrix; after union with Timbu she bears the gods Korimogo, Heyolabe, Piandela, Ni (sun) and Hela, the goddess Hana (moon), and a later generation that includes the first bird, possum and pig, hills, trees, bows and arrows, and fire and water.

sources.reference: R. M. Glasse, 'The Huli of the Southern Highlands' / Mythosphere, Huli mythology

huli_timbu.name: Sires the primordial deities upon the creator-mother Honabe
huli_timbu.notes: Male sky-being who seduces/unites with Honabe wali, fathering the first generation of Huli gods; stands above the lesser dama nature-spirits.

huli_ni.name: Gives light and warmth as the personified sun
huli_ni.notes: Huli ni, 'sun'; son of Honabe and Timbu, paired with his sister Hana the moon. Unlike the supreme Datagaliwabe, Ni and Hana are reckoned among the dama (divinities).

sources.reference: Mythosphere, Huli mythology; Glasse, Huli of the Southern Highlands

huli_hana.name: Becomes and governs the moon, the great night-light
huli_hana.notes: Huli hana, 'moon'; the one daughter among Honabe's children, an important deity paired with her brother Ni the sun. Reckoned among the dama.

sources.reference: Mythosphere, Huli mythology; Glasse, Huli of the Southern Highlands

hungarian_emese.name: Receives the founding Dream of the Turul, conceiving the royal line
hungarian_emese.notes: While pregnant she dreams that a Turul bird comes upon her and that a stream issues from her womb from which great kings will spring; her son is therefore named Álmos, 'the Dreamt One', ancestor of the Árpáds.

sources.reference: Anonymus, Gesta Hungarorum; Simon of Kéza, Gesta Hunnorum et Hungarorum

hungarian_eneh.name: Bears the twin progenitors Hunor and Magor as the totemic hind-ancestress
hungarian_eneh.notes: Wife of the giant-hunter Nimród (Ménrót); her name derives from the old Hungarian word for 'hind' (enéh/ünő), read as a survival of belief in a hind as totemic ancestress of the Magyars.

sources.reference: Simon of Kéza, Gesta Hunnorum et Hungarorum

hungarian_hunor.name: Pursues the csodaszarvas into Meotis and founds the Hun nation
hungarian_hunor.notes: Elder son of Nimród and Enéh; with his brother Magor he chases the wondrous white stag into the Meotis marshes, where the brothers settle, marry two princesses and become eponymous fathers of the Huns (Hunor) and Magyars (Magor).

sources.reference: Simon of Kéza, Gesta Hunnorum et Hungarorum

hungarian_magor.name: Follows the wondrous stag and fathers the Magyar people
hungarian_magor.notes: Younger son of Nimród and Enéh; with Hunor he pursues the csodaszarvas into the Meotis marshes and becomes the eponymous ancestor of the Magyars (Hungarians).

sources.reference: Simon of Kéza, Gesta Hunnorum et Hungarorum

ifugao_dugai.name: Bears the thunder-child Ovug to the skyworld deity Dumagid
ifugao_dugai.notes: Mortal Benguet woman, wife of Dumagid; on the journey toward the skyworld she dies as they near the sun, the loss that leads Dumagid to return and split their son Ovug into the two thunder-voices.

sources.reference: Ifugao myth, 'Origin of Thunder and Lightning' (The Aswang Project)

igbo_idemili.name: Stands as the pillar that holds up the waters, commanding rain and flood
igbo_idemili.notes: Her name glosses as 'pillar of waters'; she governs the river that bears her name through Anambra, controlling rains and floods and granting fertility.

sources.reference: Igbo oral tradition; Igbo water-divinity ethnography

hungarian_turul.name: Sword of God borne in its talons

sources.reference: Hungarian heraldic-mythological tradition (Turul depicted clutching Isten kardja)

hurrian_teshub.name: Cult of the storm-king at Kummiya, Aleppo and Tarḫuntašša
hurrian_teshub.notes: Head of the Hurrian pantheon; his mythic seat is the city of Kummiya, with major weather-god cult centres at Aleppo (Ḥalab) and across Kizzuwatna; received the storm-god's bull-offerings and oath-rites of Hittite state treaties.

sources.reference: Hurrian-Hittite cultic geography; Hittite treaty oath-lists

hurrian_hebat.name: Cult of the queen-of-heaven at Kummanni and Aleppo
hurrian_hebat.notes: Consort of Teshub, worshipped at Kummanni (classical Comana Cappadociae) and Aleppo; assimilated by the Hittites to the Sun-goddess of Arinna, an equation made explicit in Queen Puduḫepa's prayer.

sources.reference: Prayer of Puduḫepa; Hittite-Hurrian cult texts

hurrian_shaushka.name: Cult of Shaushka of Nineveh
hurrian_shaushka.notes: Her chief cult was at Nineveh and across Kizzuwatna; her statue (Ishtar of Nineveh) was twice sent to Egypt to heal Amenhotep III, per the Amarna letters. Attended in cult by her handmaidens-musicians Ninatta and Kulitta.

hurrian_sharruma.name: Cult of the mountain-god and royal protector
hurrian_sharruma.notes: Son of Teshub and Hebat, venerated in Kizzuwatna; taken by Tudḫaliya IV as personal protector-deity, who depicts the god embracing him in the Yazılıkaya rock-sanctuary (Chamber B).

sources.reference: Yazılıkaya reliefs; Hittite royal cult of Tudḫaliya IV

hurrian_kumarbi.name: Cult of the grain-father god
hurrian_kumarbi.notes: His mythic home is Urkesh, with a secondary cult centre at Azuḫinnu; addressed as a 'king' in ritual texts and named in an Assyrian takultu-text as a god of Taite alongside Nabarbi and Samanuḫa. Worship attested from Anatolia to the Zagros.

hurrian_aranzah.name: Offerings to the source of the deified Tigris
hurrian_aranzah.notes: The Tigris itself deified; first-millennium BCE Assyrian references to offerings made at the source of the Tigris in Šubria are taken to continue an earlier Hurrian worship of the river as a god.

hungarian_hadur.name: White-stallion war-sacrifice before battle
hungarian_hadur.notes: Early Magyars are said to have sacrificed white stallions to the war-god (Hadak Ura) to win his favour in war; horse-deposit burials of the 10th–13th c. attest the practice. Copper was his sacred metal.

ibeji.name: Feeding and bathing of the ere ìbejì
ibeji.notes: On the death of a twin a carved ere ìbejì is made; the mother bathes, dresses, anoints with camwood and feeds it as a living child, with offerings of ẹ̀wà ìbejì (beans) and palm-oil. Twins are held under the protection of Ṣàngó.

sources.reference: Yoruba ere ìbejì ethnography; oríkì ibeji

ibibio_ekpe.name: Ekpe (Mgbe) leopard-society masquerade and judiciary
ibibio_ekpe.notes: The bush/leopard spirit is embodied by the masked Ekpe (Mgbe/Egbo) society that served the Efik, Efut and Ibibio as judiciary, legislature and security; judgments, fines and summonses were recorded in nsibidi signs and the ukara cloth.

sources.reference: Cross River Ekpe/Mgbe society ethnography; nsibidi studies

ibibio_abasi.name: Worship through intermediaries, not direct shrine
ibibio_abasi.notes: As remote sky-creator Abasi has no temple or priesthood of his own; libations of palm-wine are poured first to Abasi Ibom, then to the ndem (marine tutelary deities), then to the ancestors (mbukpo), so the supreme god is approached through his intermediaries.

ibibio_ndem.name: Libation and offering at ndem water-shrines
ibibio_ndem.notes: The territorial marine/riverine deities are served by chief priests and priestesses; palm-wine libation, sacrifice and invocation are directed to the ndem as tutelary arch-divinities mediating between Abasi Ibom and the community.

igbo_ala.name: Iri Ji new-yam festival and mbari house
igbo_ala.notes: The earth-goddess is honoured at the new-yam festival (Iri Ji) thanking her for the harvest, and through the mbari house — a painted open-sided shrine filled with mud sculptures built to appease Ala (and Amadioha). Oath-taking and judgment of nsọ ala (abominations) fall under her.

igbo_amadioha.name: White-ram sacrifice and mbari shrine
igbo_amadioha.notes: Rituals to the thunder-god centre on sacrifice of a white ram (his sacred animal and emblem); shrines hold an iron staff and ram-horns, and major mbari houses were built to him alongside Ala. His colours are red (wrath) and white (purity); nzu chalk marks truth in his rites.

igbo_idemili.name: Veneration of the royal python (éké Idemili)
igbo_idemili.notes: In the Idemili clan the royal python is sacred to the goddess as her living messenger; to kill one is a grave abomination requiring a human-style burial for the snake to avert her wrath.

igbo_ikenga.name: Personal Ikenga shrine of the right hand
igbo_ikenga.notes: Each man keeps a carved Ikenga as a shrine to his right hand (aka ikenga); it is fed daily with kola and palm-wine and, before an important undertaking, with the sacrificial blood of a cock or ram. Over years it accretes residue of blood, chewed kola and alligator pepper.

igbo_agwu.name: Daily dibia devotion and Nsọ/Iwu Agwụ observance
igbo_agwu.notes: Every dibia prays to Agwu at first rising and observes the Nsọ Agwụ (taboos) and Iwu Agwụ (laws) of the deity; possession by Agwu is what makes a diviner-healer, and its neglect brings madness and confusion.

sources.reference: J. C. U. Aguwa, The Agwu Deity in Igbo Religion

igbo_chukwu.name: Arochukwu oracle (Ibini Ukpabi / Long Juju)
igbo_chukwu.notes: Though the supreme creator was held to need no shrine, his voice was sought at the Ibini Ukpabi oracle in a sacred cave at Arochukwu, the most powerful oracle in precolonial Igboland; dibia priests interpreted its pronouncements with palm fronds and kola. Destroyed by the British in the Aro Expedition of 1901–02.

igbo_ekwensu.name: Ekwensu war-festival and Mgbedike masquerade
igbo_ekwensu.notes: Communities such as Onicha-Ukwuani and the Obollo (during the onwa-asaa festival) honour Ekwensu in memory of victories in war, with forest shrines and masquerade. The fierce horned-and-tusked Mgbedike mask embodies him as warrior-god of the wilderness. He is a trickster-spirit, not a Christian devil.

sources.reference: Igbo cosmology; Ekwensu festival and Mgbedike masquerade ethnography

ijaw_adumu.name: Owu water-spirit masquerade of the Ekine (Sekiapu) society
ijaw_adumu.notes: The owuamapu water-spirits, headed by Adumu (Kalabari Owu), are served by the Ekine (Sekiapu) society, whose masked dancers wear human-and-aquatic crest headdresses to embody them; the Owu-Aru-Sun festival marks their cyclic return.

ijaw_egbesu.name: Egbesu war-rites and just-cause protection
ijaw_egbesu.notes: The Egbesu force may be invoked only in defence or to right an injustice, by those in harmony with the cosmos; priests (e.g. the Olodiama Egbesu) perform peri rites, and the deity comes out as the Egbesu Owu masquerade. His emblems are the leopard, panther and lion.

attributes.name: Strides wielding a mace or double axe and a triple thunderbolt
attributes.notes: Standard storm-god pose: stepping forward on mountains or on a bull, brandishing axe/mace in one hand and forked lightning in the other.

sources.reference: Anatolian-Hurrian storm-god iconography (Yazılıkaya; IDD Anatolia/N. Syria)

attributes.name: Horned crown marking divine and bovine power

sacredAnimals.name: The bulls Šeri and Ḫurri who draw his chariot or bear him

attributes.name: Matronly queen enthroned or standing on her lion
attributes.notes: In the Yazılıkaya procession she heads the goddesses, seated on a lion (or shown standing upon it).

attributes.name: Winged goddess standing on the back of a lion
attributes.notes: Often shown with wings and accompanied by two birds (doves); in Anatolia linked to the awiti winged-lion/sphinx.

sacredAnimals.name: Lion (mount) and a pair of doves

attributes.name: Young god in tunic and pointed shoes, riding a leopard or holding a lance
attributes.notes: May also appear theriomorphic as a bull; his sign is a pair of human legs or a human head on a bull's body.

sources.reference: Yazılıkaya Chamber B relief; Hurrian-Hittite iconography

attributes.name: Winged god whose pointed cap bears the lunar crescent
attributes.notes: Portrayed identically with a crescent-topped pointed cap and wings on the shoulders; god of the moon, oaths, oracles and pregnancy.

attributes.name: Solar god associated with the winged sun-disk who surveys all the earth
attributes.notes: Equated with Šamaš/Utu; like the Mesopotamian sun-god seen as all-seeing arbiter; the winged disk that doubles as the Hittite royal emblem 'My Sun'.

sources.reference: Mesopotamian-Hurrian solar iconography; Hittite winged-disk studies

attributes.name: Bears the primeval copper saw that once split heaven and earth
attributes.notes: In the Song of Ullikummi Ea produces this ancient cutting tool to sever the stone monster from Upelluri's shoulder, breaking its invulnerability.

attributes.name: Falcon/hawk of prey with wings spread, often gripping a sword
attributes.notes: Rendered as a stylized raptor with hooked beak and sharp talons on the shields and crests of Attila, Álmos and Árpád; commonly shown clutching the Sword of God.

sources.reference: Hungarian chronicle and heraldic tradition (Gesta Hungarorum; Simon of Kéza)

sacredAnimals.name: The falcon/eagle bird-of-prey itself, the theriomorphic ancestor-spirit

attributes.name: Mighty long-haired warrior in armour and weapons of pure copper
attributes.notes: Copper is his sacred metal; depicted brandishing a sword or spear. As smith of the gods he forged the Sword of God (Isten kardja) later wielded by Attila.

sources.reference: Hungarian mythology (Ipolyi, Magyar Mythologia; literary tradition)

attributes.name: The half-being whose voice is thunder — sharp from the skyworld half, low from the earth half
attributes.notes: Split down the middle by his father Dumagid: the skyworld-Ovug's voice is sharp lightning-thunder, the earth-Ovug's voice is low rolling-thunder.

sources.reference: Ifugao myth, 'Origin of Thunder and Lightning'

attributes.name: Enthroned mother-goddess in mud sculpture, often with a child
attributes.notes: In the mbari house she is shown as a seated woman, frequently holding or flanked by a small child and a python; the crescent moon is among her symbols.

sacredAnimals.name: The python (éké), her living agent on earth

attributes.name: Red-and-white emblem — red for wrath, white for purity and order
attributes.notes: His shrine displays ram-horns, an iron staff, and a white cloth; nzu (white chalk) marks truth in his rites.

sacredAnimals.name: The white ram, his sacred animal and the form in which he appears

attributes.name: Carved figure crowned with two curved ram's horns (opi)
attributes.notes: The horns are its most characteristic element — 'the ram goes into a fight head first' — the right hand (aka ikenga) holds a machete or sword, the left a trophy such as a severed head, tusk or money-bag.

sacredAnimals.name: The royal python (éké Idemili), her sacred emblem and messenger
The vulture, her earthly representation at sacrifice
sacredAnimals.notes: A vulture's presence at a sacrifice is read as the sign that Abasi has accepted the offering, marking Atai's role as bridge between divine and earthly.

attributes.name: Leopard masquerade with blue-and-white ukara cloth inscribed in nsibidi
attributes.notes: The Ekpe initiate's regalia bears nsibidi ideographs; the leopard (ekpe/mgbe) is the society's totem and the spirit's manifest form.

sources.reference: Cross River Ekpe society; nsibidi studies

sacredAnimals.name: The leopard, the spirit's totem animal
Leopard, panther and lion — the symbols of the war-deity's force
